design.question: Does the tumour-naive fragmentomics model, trained on FinaleDB publications 6+8, track the tumour fraction in a colorectal cohort it has never seen, and does it separate CRC from benign plasma there?
design.harmonization: per study on the training side, per publication on the held-out side
design.primary_readout: the tumour-fraction gradient, not a cancer/control AUC

cohort.build: hg38 -- the build the feature grid uses

library.note: The held-out cohort's library has a different fragment-size shape from the training cohort's, so the per-cohort harmonisation carries a real shift. The ranking is the honest number here; the absolute threshold is not.

format.columns: chrom, start, end, score, strand (the fragment form the extractor reads)
format.build: hg38 -- the build the extractor's bin grid uses, so no conversion and no grid loss
format.note: The depositor built these files with `cut -f1,2,6,8,9` on a BEDPE, so the outer coordinates are start1 and end2; the check above establishes that no row is an inverted interval, which would have made the extractor drop that fragment silently.

result.crc_vs_benign_note: Reported for completeness and close to meaningless on its own: the two benign samples carry a tumour fraction of 0.0062-0.0072 and three CRC samples carry 0.0049-0.4029, so the contrast is between a low tumour fraction and a slightly different low tumour fraction. The gradient and the longitudinal series are what this cohort carries.

score_saturation.note: Whether the model's scores sit at the top of its range in this cohort, as they did in the PHTS cohort. See harmonization_sensitivity for the control that does not let the cohort normalise itself.

longitudinal_series.note: Same patient, same laboratory, rising tumour fraction. A cohort shift cannot move this comparison.

verdict.question: Does the tumour-naive fragmentomics model track the tumour fraction in colorectal plasma, over an eighty-fold range of it, at the training cohort's own depth and genome build?
verdict.answer: the score's Spearman rho against the tumour fraction is 0.6611 (permutation p 0.064147), so it does not track it at this n; within the CRC samples alone rho is 0.8154 (p 0.035548); and the longitudinal series is not monotone

limits: Nine samples. The gradient's Spearman rho over nine points has a wide interval, and the longitudinal series is three draws of one patient. Both are measurements.

The cancer/control contrast in this cohort is close to meaningless on its own -- the benign samples carry a tumour fraction of the same order as the lowest CRC samples -- so the AUC must not be read as a detection result.
One patient supplies the longitudinal series, so the comparison cannot be generalised beyond him; what it can do is show whether the score moves with his own tumour burden.
The tumour fraction is the depositor's, and it is a fraction of the reads assigned to the tumour; it is used here as the dose axis, not as a label the model is allowed to see.
